Author: @slipperybogles
Content:
What Muta conveniently leaves out in this video is that MGS3 is notoriously tough to emulate, it made heavy use of the PS2's analog face buttons for different inputs. Controllers don't have analog face buttons anymore, very few games made use of them and the feature was scrapped. 
Your options for emulating are either

A. get a DualShock 3 (the last controller to have analog face buttons) as well as the software required to connect it to your pc
or
B. bind a button to be a "pressure modifier" which you can hold to get those alternate inputs form the face buttons, however MGS3 makes use of every button on the controller, so you'll have to unbind an "unimportant" button and lose it's function in the game

Neither of these options are convenient, it's so much easier to just buy the remaster where the controls have been reprogrammed to work on a modern controller. 
I don't understand why muta constantly gasses up emulators as some universal band-aid to bad rereleases without ever bringing up the obstacles people will face when they try to emulate these games.

Content:
Posted this in a comment thread below, but wanted more opinions on this, so double posting it here.

UE5 is a problem to an extent, yes. Theres clearly a trend of UE5 games having consistent issues, however the real problem is still publishers pushing unrealistic deadlines to Devs, to satisfy stake holders. 

UE5 games can be optimized too, however currently its being used for quantity over quality. Developers are able to make modern looking games with amazing effects and graphics, with much less effort and time. 

Honestly I truly believe the real problem with optimization in gaming is that tech stake holders refuse to give enough wiggle room to increase the industry standard of 5 years development time for AAA titles. At minimum nowadays, to meet modern demands and expectations of gamers, it should be 6 years, if not 7. So when a publisher decides to invest into a new title, regardless of scope they still try to hit that 5 year mark, and it causes optimization to take a back seat to the rest of development.

Author: @Zadamanim
Content: It makes no sense to use UE5's Lumen system in a game like MGS3. Lumen is good if you need to have hundreds of light sources that can be controlled individually (to move, change color, or turn on/off) or if the environment is highly destructible. When the map is unchanging with a single, unchanging primary light source (the sun) and occasional lights from explosions, you have the worst case scenario for running Lumen. It's going to run way worse than a normal lighting solution would.

Author: @zephranarx2172
Content:
"UE5 is a blight on the industry"

I've ranted about it once, I'll rant about it again, UE is just.. Horrible with optimization. They try to push these "AI tools" to manage optimization (like AI culling, AI to handle LoDs without having to force you to make your own low-poly models, and even AI to handle lighting.)

The problem with these AI tools? They suck. Simply put.
They're only effective on "very poorly optimized" games. I.E. models that have way too many triangles and need a reduction, and such. Which, by that point, if you're using an AI to fix that, just stop developing games, please.
When these tools are used on games where people actually tried to optimize their game? (You know, by using baked lighting, manually using Blender to reduce triangles, setting up your own LoDs) They actually make the performance like 40% worse.

So yeah.
If you're a game dev and are considering using UE, uh..
*Do everyone a favor and don't.*

hey mutah.... are you talking out ur neck? unreal engine, unity or any other game engine has nothing to do with metal gear. i thought most of the fans knew kojima san and his team hand constructed the fox engine. idk maybe im a uber fan i guess. but since you didnt feel like doing your due dilligence, here ya go. or i guess your talking about konami's end of the spectrum. sorry, no offense brother mutah
The Fox Engine is a proprietary game engine built entirely by Kojima Productions in-house, using C++ as the primary programming language, to develop cross-platform games with significantly shortened development times and reduced costs. It features a focus on photorealism and is built around rendering using real-world scanned assets, linear-space lighting, and physically-based rendering to achieve high-quality graphics.
 
Key aspects of the Fox Engine:
Proprietary technology:
The engine was developed exclusively by Kojima Productions and is not licensed from another company. 
Cross-platform focus:
It was designed to enable developers to create multiplatform games more easily, moving away from single-platform development. 
Photorealistic rendering:
A major emphasis was placed on achieving photo-realism by translating physical objects and images into the engine, using techniques like deferred rendering and physically-based rendering. 
High-quality assets:
The engine was built to render highly detailed, scanned models rather than hand-created ones, and textures were rendered from real photographs, not created from scratch. 
Development approach:
The goal was to create a highly responsive and clean engine that allowed for detailed open-world environments, dynamic lighting, and complex physics and AI systems. 
In short, the Fox Engine was Konami's (specifically Kojima Productions') answer to creating a powerful, multi-platform engine focused on realistic visuals and efficient development. Konami has since discontinued its use in favor of Unreal Engine 5 for newer titles, such as the upcoming Metal Gear Solid Delta.

Content: 30 feels fine if a game is designed around 30, and even then it can feel bad depending on the genre. Even ps2 games from 2002 like ratchet and clank ran at 60 fps and were packed with content on screen, they did this for tons of games. The ps4 remake felt horrible at 30. Everything felt slow. There are some games that even feel slow at 60, but i feel its a case of “if you dont know, you wont realize” over 60 fps. I eventually went from a 60hz 1080p to a 240hz 1440p monitor. Lowering my fps by switching between or lowering the monitors fps (which makes it feel worse than the actual low fps due to how ips monitors work) is jarring and suddenly u feel like nothing is responsive. But then come back a few hours later and it feels fine again. Same cant be said for 30 which feels bad either way unless its a slow paced game built around it. We need to stop making games run like garbage when its intended for a specific device like a console.
